title: Joe Oliver, New Orleans historians, and the 1936 reorganization
summary: La Rocca says Oliver and the Louisiana Five took from the band's records, attacks pro-Negro historians and Marshall Stearns, and says Tom Brown made untrue claims when the band was reorganized in 1936.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: You know, that's all. Not only the Louisiana Five, but everybody. It was a field lead from the all steel music and different things out the original Dixieland jazz band. Now they say these Negroes didn't hear these records. Joe heard them. If this man heard them, Joe Oliver heard them. Because Joe, in his thing, that's what he bases his rhythm on. Because he didn't know no better. He was just a Negro that didn't know no better. Like these even white crumbs who's supposed to be historians around New Orleans. They can't be honest people. I have a statement in one of the second line about Miss Myra Manfeld. She says, it never rains, but it pours. Marshall Stein is in town with the Guggenheimer Foundation. Well, this ain't a laugh. This is a laugh. She says, whenever they come to find out of jazz, I see that they go see the right people. Now here's a woman, maybe in 40 years of age, interested in herself to be pro-Negro. Marshall Stein, who is a pro-Negro, and is the cause of integration of bands, and is the cause of softening the morals of the integrated people of the South. This man belongs to a society, a young man's Christian Hebrew Association. He has it on his letter. I'd like to read that letter to you, or have someone read it for me. All right. To bring you up to date on this thing, this happened in 1936, when I was to reorganize the band, and this Tom Brown had given a lot of information that was untrue. He said he had the first original Dixieland jazz band, but he didn't make no claims at this time of composing any numbers. That came later. When he got mixed with Sushon, that all came up later, about the numbers that he had composed. But I want you to read that.
